slides.texte_overlay:
7 subtle behaviors that make
people take you seriously
Pause before you answer. Someone asks you a question, count one second in your head, then reply. It looks like you're actually thinking, and people trust an answer that wasn't rushed out.

Use people's names when it matters. "Mark, I hear you, but I see it differently." Saying a name calmly in a tense moment makes you sound grounded, not defensive. It changes the whole tone of the talk.
Keep learning in silence. Five minutes a day of history, art or science. Nobody needs to know you do it. They just notice that you always seem to understand what's going on.
slides.texte_sophia: I started doing five minutes a day on a micro-learning app like the Sophia app. History, art, science. Nobody knows I do it. They just notice I always seem to understand what's going on.

slides.texte_overlay: Keep your face relaxed when you listen. No nervous nodding, no forced smile every two seconds. A calm, attentive face says you're secure. Constant nodding says you need the other person to like you.
Arrive a few minutes early. Sit down, settle in, look around before the meeting starts. The guy who rushes in late and out of breath never gets taken as seriously as the one who was already there.

Don't fill every silence. When you've made your point, stop talking. No "you know what I mean?" at the end. Letting your words land without explaining them twice is one of the strongest signals there is.

Write things down. In a meeting, at the doctor, when your boss gives feedback. Taking notes tells people you take them seriously, and people take you seriously back. It's that simple, and almost nobody does it.
